sections.html:
A quitclaim deed hands over whatever interest the signer holds and promises nothing about its quality. It does not clear a mortgage, a tax lien or a co-owner's share, so it suits people who already trust the title.

Arkansas law is picky about the paper. The conveyance must be acknowledged, the county recorder has to accept the format, and a married owner's homestead pulls the spouse into the signing. Each point gets its own section below.

A recorder can refuse a deed that breaks the format rules in Ark. Code 14-15-402. A missed margin is enough to send a deed back.

  • Paper size is 8.5 by 11 inches.
  • Leave 2.5 inches of blank space at the top right of the first page for the file mark.
  • Sides and bottom need 0.5 inch, and the last page needs 2.5 inches at the bottom.
  • The document carries its title and the names of grantor and grantee.
  • It must be legible and acknowledged under 16-47-207.

The recorder can waive the format for good cause. Documents signed before January 1, 2004, plus plats and surveys, are exempt from the format rules.

Section 14-15-403 adds a second requirement: the preparer's name and address on the first page of any instrument affecting title. If a recorder accepts a noncompliant instrument, the fee is refundable on request within six months, and the instrument still gives notice. Wills, court decrees and instruments signed before August 1, 1959 are exempt.

sections.h2: Does a spouse have to sign a quitclaim on a homestead?
sections.html:
Yes. When the property is the homestead of a married person, the spouse must join in the deed or sign a separate acknowledged deed. Under Ark. Code 18-12-403, an instrument affecting that homestead has no validity without the spouse's participation.

Taxes, laborers' and mechanics' liens, and purchase money are the exceptions. Section 18-12-202 lets a married person acknowledge a conveyance of their own property, or release dower, curtesy or homestead in a spouse's property, as if unmarried, with no separate examination.

A quitclaim signed by one spouse alone can leave a hole in the title. If the house was a homestead, ask the title company whether the other spouse must sign.

Recording cures some acknowledgment defects, but do not plan around that. Section 18-12-208 names defects that will not defeat a recorded instrument.

  • A missing or wrong notary seal, on deeds signed after August 13, 1993.
  • A missing or wrong commission expiration date.
  • A wrong date or a missing county.
  • A notary who moved out of the commissioning county.
  • Wording that departs from the statutory form but makes a good-faith attempt at material compliance.

A defective but recorded deed still gives constructive notice of its contents. For instruments recorded on or after April 8, 2013, a proper jurat can stand in for an acknowledgment certificate.

The circuit clerk, who serves as recorder, charges fees set by statute. Under Ark. Code 21-6-306, Pulaski County charges $15 for the first page of a deed and $5 for each added page. Other counties post their own schedules, so call the clerk where the land sits.

ChargeAmount
Deed, first page (Pulaski County)$15.00
Each added page$5.00
Document non-compliance fee$25.00 per document, plus page fees
State transfer tax, base (Ark. Code 26-60-105(a))$1.10 per $1,000
State transfer tax, added (Ark. Code 26-60-105(b))$2.20 per $1,000, paid by purchaser

Together the two tax pieces make $3.30 per $1,000 of consideration, and the tax applies only when consideration is over $100. The Miscellaneous Tax Section sells the transfer stamps and answers questions at 501-682-7187.

sections.h2: Quitclaim deeds exempt from transfer tax
sections.html:
Several kinds of transfer are exempt, and a family quitclaim may fit one. Section 26-60-102 lists twelve categories, including these:

  • Property divided between divorcing parties.
  • Instruments given only to secure a debt, and certain transfers to a secured party enforcing a security interest.
  • Corrections of a recorded instrument when tax was already paid.
  • Land sold for delinquent taxes.
  • Beneficiary deeds under 18-12-608.
  • Transfers to or from governments, and some business entity reorganizations.

A FHA, VA or USDA Rural Development home is exempt if the price is $60,000 or less and the seller files a sworn statement that the buyer and spouse have owned no home in the prior three years. A plain gift between relatives is a different matter, so call the state revenue office before assuming an exemption.

To pass a house at death, a beneficiary deed is often cleaner because it does nothing until the owner dies. Ark. Code 18-12-608 says it must state that it is not effective until death, and it is valid only if recorded with the county recorder before the owner dies.

  • The owner can revoke it any time with a signed, recorded revocation. A will cannot revoke it.
  • If several deeds exist, the last one signed before death controls, whatever the recording order.
  • The transfer stays subject to mortgages, liens and leases that exist at death.
  • For joint tenants or spouses holding by the entirety, all surviving owners must sign.

A beneficiary deed is also exempt from the transfer tax. A quitclaim to a child during life hands over a present interest, so talk to a lawyer before choosing.

Take the checks in the order the statutes create them, so the recorder has nothing to reject.

  • Confirm every owner and whether the house is a married person's homestead.
  • Put the preparer's name and address on the first page, and leave the file-mark space at the top right.
  • Sign before a notary, with the acknowledgment naming the state and county.
  • Check for a transfer tax exemption, and buy stamps if none applies.
  • Record the deed with the recorder in the county where the property is located, and keep the receipt.

sections.h2: When a quitclaim complicates a sale
sections.html:
A buyer's title company may question the gap a quitclaim leaves. Usual trouble spots are a missing spouse signature, a mortgage still in the old owner's name, and unpaid property tax.

The tax lien binds the house and ranks ahead of other liens under 26-34-101, so a deed between family does not move the tax debt away. Cash Home Buyers makes as-is offers on Arkansas houses, including houses where a quitclaim was recorded. If one is already recorded on your house, have the recorded copy and any mortgage statement ready when you call.

faqs.q: Does a quitclaim deed guarantee clear title?
faqs.a: No. It passes only the interest the signer holds and promises nothing about liens, co-owners or defects. A mortgage or tax lien stays on the property after a quitclaim.

faqs.q: Does my spouse have to sign if I quitclaim our home?
faqs.a: Yes, if it is your homestead. Section 18-12-403 voids a homestead instrument unless the spouse joins or signs a separate acknowledged deed, with exceptions for taxes, certain liens and purchase money.

faqs.q: How much does it cost to record a deed in Arkansas?
faqs.a: Pulaski County charges $15 for the first page and $5 for each additional page. Other counties post their own schedules, so ask the circuit clerk in the county where the land is.

faqs.q: What is the Arkansas real estate transfer tax rate?
faqs.a: It is $3.30 per $1,000 of consideration on transfers above $100: $1.10 base plus $2.20 paid by the purchaser. Divorce divisions, security deeds and beneficiary deeds are among the exemptions.

faqs.q: Can I use a quitclaim to transfer a house to my child at death?
faqs.a: A beneficiary deed under 18-12-608 is built for that. It must state that it takes effect at death and be recorded before the owner dies.
